report:
## Conclusion

**No—arthroscopy generally does not help knee osteoarthritis.** Arthroscopic “washout,” debridement (smoothing/removing damaged tissue), or similar procedures do not provide meaningful, lasting improvement in pain or function beyond well-delivered nonsurgical treatment such as exercise-based physical therapy and medicines.

A randomized controlled trial found that adding arthroscopic surgery to optimized physical and medical therapy gave **no additional benefit** for knee osteoarthritis. Major guidelines therefore advise against arthroscopy with lavage/debridement when symptomatic knee OA is the primary diagnosis. The AAOS rates this recommendation as moderate-strength; the BMJ expert guideline makes a strong recommendation against arthroscopy for nearly all people with degenerative knee disease (OA and/or degenerative meniscal tears).

This conclusion does **not** apply to every knee problem: arthroscopy may still be considered for a separate, specific indication—for example, a true mechanically locked knee caused by a displaced tear or loose body, or an acute traumatic injury. Those decisions require assessment by an orthopaedic clinician. For OA itself, focus should usually be on tailored exercise/strengthening, weight management where relevant, pain-relief options, and discussion of joint replacement only when symptoms remain severe despite comprehensive conservative care.

**Sources**

1. AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline, *Management of Osteoarthritis of the Knee (Non-Arthroplasty)*: https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf  
2. Kirkley et al., randomized trial (PubMed): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18784099/  
3. BMJ clinical practice guideline: https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982  
4. NICE, *Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management*: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng226/chapter/Recommendations
